clips.text: Snow throws back 80 percent of the sun's burning light — how did bone save his sight?
Because the first sunglasses had no glass. Only bone — and a slit so narrow it lets almost no light in.
Next: the glare, the carving, and the trick that makes less light mean sharper sight. Stay with me.
This is the moment after. A hunter stands on the spring ice at dawn, the sun low and white — and he is about to walk a whole day across a mirror that burns.
You know this glare. Fresh snow on a bright day, your eyes watering before you even reach the door. Now take away the door, the shade, the trees — and walk on it all day.
He has no glass. No plastic, no dark lenses, nothing bought. He has a strip of bone, a knife, and a trick older than the first pair of spectacles by two thousand years.
So here is the story, and it starts now. One hunter, one day on the ice, and a pair of glasses with no glass in them. The glare is first.
Chapter one: midday. The sun is high now — and the ice below you is a second sun.
Count the dose. Fresh snow throws back about 80 percent of the burning light that hits it. Sand throws back 15 percent. Sea foam, 25. Snow is not a surface. It is a mirror aimed at your eyes.
And the dose comes from below, where no hat brim reaches. Your eyes take the sun twice — once from the sky, once from the ground. There is no shade to step into, because the ground itself is shining.

Climb higher and it gets worse. The burning light grows about 10 to 12 percent stronger for every thousand metres you climb. Up here, the air is thinner, the sun is harder, and the ice is brighter still.
Thirty minutes. That is all the burning light needs to start hurting your eyes — half an hour, unprotected, on a bright day. You will not feel it. Not yet. That is the trap.

Because the burn does not arrive when the light hits. It arrives six to twelve hours later — in the evening, in the dark, when the day is done. Your eyes feel fine all day. Then night falls, and they catch fire.
So the hunter has a problem with no warning and no mercy. The burn comes hours after the cause, when it is far too late to hide. The answer is in his hands — a strip of bone, and a knife.
Chapter two: afternoon. He stops, sits on the ice, and carves. A strip of bone, cut to fit his own face.

The goggles have a name. In Inuktitut they are called ilgaak. In Yupik, nigaugek. They are not bought. They are carved — from bone, walrus ivory, caribou antler, driftwood, whatever the Arctic hands you.
He cuts the strip to the shape of his face, so it sits tight, with no gaps at the edges. A cord of caribou sinew holds it on. And then he cuts the slit — one thin horizontal line for each eye.
The slit is the whole trick. It is just wide enough to see through, and narrow enough to block almost everything else. The goggles do not filter the light. They shut most of it out.
Then he blackens the inside with soot — rubbed in, so the bone itself stops shining. Some hunters rub soot or gunpowder on the outside too. Every surface that could throw light back is turned black.

And the Yupik had a cleverer version. Instead of one slit, many — thin slits stacked like a Venetian blind, giving a wider view while still cutting the glare. Same bone, same trick, more light to see by.
He ties them on, and the world goes dark — then sharp. The glare is gone. The ice is still there, every crack of it, but the burning is cut to a sliver. He can walk again.
So the goggles work. But here is the part that should not work — and does. The slit does not just protect his eyes. It makes them sharper. The next chapter is the trick inside the trick.
Chapter three: dusk. The paradox. Less light — sharper sight. How can blocking light make you see better?
Try it yourself. Squint at something far away, and it sharpens. Your eyelids narrow the opening, and the blur tightens. The goggles do the same thing — a squint carved in bone, held in place all day.
It works like a pinhole camera. A tiny opening lets only the straightest rays through, and the picture on the other side comes out sharper. The slit is a pinhole — and your eye is the camera.

And the numbers back it up. A Danish eye doctor named Mogens Norn tested old goggles in the 1990s, and found they cut the burning light down to between 2 and 8 percent. Ninety-two to ninety-eight percent of it — gone.
That is the double trick. The slit blocks the burn — and focuses the picture. One cut in bone does both jobs at once. No glass, no chemistry, no moving parts. Just geometry.

An anthropologist named Ann Fienup-Riordan found out by accident. After eye surgery, she tried on a pair of Yupik goggles — and the distant landscape snapped into focus. She said, I could see. The goggles corrected her sight, like a prescription.
The elders knew it all along. They said the narrow slits sharpen and focus vision, like a pinhole camera. The science came two thousand years later — and agreed with them.
So the slit is not a compromise. It is not seeing less so you can survive. It is seeing better BECAUSE you let less in. The glare was never the light you needed — it was the light in the way.
But how old is this trick, really? The next chapter is the proof — the oldest eyewear we know of, dug out of the frozen ground.
Chapter four: evening. The proof. These are the oldest sunglasses on Earth — and they are two thousand years old.

Pairs carved from walrus ivory have been found in Old Bering Sea sites nearly two thousand years old. One Yupik pair in the Smithsonian lets light in through nine narrow slits — and nowhere else. Nine slits, no glass, two thousand years.

Guinness calls them the first sunglasses. The oldest examples date to around the first century — thin masks of wood or bone, pierced with thin horizontal slits, worn across the Arctic in Alaska, Canada, Greenland, and Siberia.

Some evidence pushes the idea further back — closer to four thousand years, to the earliest Arctic settlements. The honest date is a range: about two thousand years for sure, maybe twice that. Either way, they predate glass lenses by more than a thousand years.
And they never went away. Hunters still carve them and wear them today — bone, antler, wood, whale baleen, even seashore grass. The design has not changed, because the problem has not changed.

Modern glacier glasses are the same idea in plastic — side shields, dark lenses, the same tight fit against the face. The material changed. The geometry did not. A slit in bone became a lens in a frame — but the job is identical.
So here is the question the whole story turns on: if the first sunglasses had no glass — only a slit of bone — what else did we invent twice, once in bone and once in glass?
The verdict. Tonight, the story closes like this. The first sunglasses had no glass — and they worked better than glass, in the one place glass could not go.

The proof is a strip of bone, a slit, and a hunter who walked a whole day across a burning mirror. Eighty percent of the light thrown back — cut to between 2 and 8 percent. And the picture, sharper, not duller.

But remember the price. The slit narrows your world. No peripheral vision, no wide view — you see a thin band of the world, and the rest is bone. You trade width for safety, and you pay it every hour you wear them.

If you had to cross a blinding white ice field with only a strip of bone and a knife — would you cut the slit wide, for a better view, or narrow, for safer eyes? Tell us where you would draw the line.

Science note, plainly. The 80 percent figure is for fresh snow, against ultraviolet light — sand throws back about 15 percent, sea foam about 25. The 2 to 8 percent comes from Norn's 1990s tests on museum goggles, not a universal constant. The age is a range — about two thousand years for sure, maybe up to four thousand.

My sources, to check me: Guinness World Records, on the first sunglasses, around the first century; Wikipedia, on snow blindness — onset six to twelve hours, healing in 24 to 72 hours; Mogens Norn, in the 1990s, on the 2 to 8 percent; and the Smithsonian, on the nine-slit Yupik pair and the elders who said the slits sharpen vision like a pinhole camera.

Snow throws back 80 percent of the sun's burning light — and bone saved his sight. Thank the hunters who carved the first sunglasses, the elders who knew the slit sharpened sight, and the anthropologist who could see again.
The light was always the problem — and the answer was never more light. It was less. Goodnight. And if you step onto bright snow tomorrow — remember, the ground is a second sun.
